title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Tuesday morning, Nov 24
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 7:20 AM ET Tuesday, Nov 24, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). New and on top: Trump's Justice Department attack on Gov. Gavin Newsom's commutation of all 548 California death sentences ('he stood with the murderers and the child slayers'): 8,000 posts in 24 hours, 12.59× its prior daily average, 6,227 of them overnight, and 'Newscum' was a U.S. trend. Election-doubt claims grew overnight: the Michigan 'Chinese Wi-Fi radio next to a Dominion tabulator' claim reached 12,072 posts (7,074 from 5 PM to 7 AM ET, versus 4 a night earlier) even as Michigan certified its results, and the forensic-audit demand hit 12,865 (7,623 overnight versus 5,408) as Mike Lindell called the midterms 'the biggest theft.' Also new on the Right: 'Democrats will raise your taxes' after Rep. Richard Neal's hearings plan (4,532 posts, 2.86×). The 'fine people hoax' cooled overnight (2,868 versus 8,427). On the Far Left, Medicare for All is still the largest query (16,901 posts) but is back to its weekly average, and Van Hollen vs. Schumer cooled (4,563). One faded card was dropped and two were added. Every count, quote and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this morning or carried over from last evening and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

trends.detail: U.S. trends were pulled at about 7:07 AM ET with x.get_trends_by_woeid (WOEID 23424977, max 50; 41 returned). Monday Night Football and morning trends dominated: 'Commanders' (65,228 posts), 'Out of Time' (63,015), 'Bengals' (62,217), 'Edwin' (48,291), 'Good Tuesday' (35,109) and 'Burrow' (33,100). 'Newscum' (2,790), Trump's nickname for Gov. Gavin Newsom, matches the new death-row card; a sample of 'Newscum' posts since 7 PM ET Monday was almost entirely about the commutations, so that card gets the trend bonus. 'Cenk' (6,708) and 'DeNiro' (1,211) were also on the list; we did not match them to a card. Where a trend object had no tweet_count ('#iskadiyebiri,' '#ReasonableDoubtHulu,' 'AFC North,' '#HTTC,' '#HTTR'), its volume is unavailable and we did not estimate it.

Carried over from last evening: Lead Stories, plus the Election Crime Bureau's claim post, Badlands Media's CISA report and SmokeScreen's write-up (cited, not counted) (new Michigan Wi-Fi card); FactCheck.org and PolitiFact, plus a Truth Social archive (cited, not counted) (new Somali–Minnesota card); Mediaite ('fine people'); USA Today (Medicare for All); the New York Post, plus the NYC Mayor's Office plan (cited, not counted) (Rikers); and AP, cited on the audit card for the separate RNC spending audit fight (not added to its count). Earlier outlets carried on each card are listed in its sources.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The Rikers card is a Right attack on a Democratic mayor; we include it because Mamdani is being used as the national face of the party. The market card is tagged Right because the 'Democrats crashed the market' frame comes from Trump and his Treasury Secretary, even though many posts matching the query are rebuttals. The Rubio card recasts the incoming majority as Marxist, using a 2020 video. The 'fine people' card is tagged Right because it uses a Fox co-host's comment to brand Democrats as liars; it is about a 2017 quote, not the midterms. The Medicare for All card is tagged Far Left because the pressure is on Jeffries, Schumer and the incoming majority to deliver it now. The Van Hollen card is tagged Far Left because the push to replace Schumer comes from the party's left. The tag is the primary opposition frame. The Michigan Wi-Fi card is tagged Right because the claim casts doubt on an election Democrats won. The Somali–Minnesota card is tagged Right because it is Trump's attack on a community in a Democratic-run state. The new Newsom death-row card is tagged Right because it is the administration's attack on a Democratic governor and potential 2028 candidate. The new tax card is tagged Right because 'Democrats will raise your taxes' is the Right's reading of a hearings plan; no bill exists yet.

methodology: Last updated Tuesday, Nov 24, 2026, 7:20 AM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 7:07 AM ET. Last evening's snapshot (Nov 23, 5:30 PM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Nine of its ten narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps last evening's by 10 hours (7 AM to 5 PM Monday ET), so we also report each query's 5 PM–7 AM ET overnight count against the same hours a night earlier. One narrative was dropped because it faded: the Rahm Emanuel–DSA card (403 posts in the last 24 hours, down from 805 last evening; 84 from 5 PM to 7 AM ET versus 483 the same hours a night earlier). Two were added with new queries: the Newsom death-row attack and 'Democrats will raise your taxes.' Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: progressive criticism of Hakeem Jeffries over Israel and donors (3,986 posts, 0.38× its prior daily average, falling) and claims that California's House sweep was fraudulent (135 posts, 0.69×), which X News covered but which barely registered in counts. Rep. Robert Garcia's resurfaced 'impeachable offenses weekly' clip and the federal probe involving Rep. Ilhan Omar's former aide were covered by X News but not counted this morning.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent twice: at daily granularity over a 167-hour window from 8:00 AM ET Tuesday, Nov 17, through 7:00 AM ET Tuesday, Nov 24 (the 'seven-day' total), and at hourly granularity over the last 24 hours (7:00 AM ET Monday, Nov 23, through 7:00 AM ET Tuesday, Nov 24). We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official government pages, transcripts, advocacy groups, blogs, aggregators, archives, X News summaries and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets; this morning that includes the White House, the Michigan Department of State, the U.S. Election Assistance Commission and Read The American. This morning we researched the two new cards and re-researched the 'fine people,' Medicare for All, audit, Michigan Wi-Fi and Somali–Minnesota cards; the market, Rubio, Van Hollen and Rikers cards carry last evening's outlet counts and say so. One topic in this set, the Newsom card ('Newscum'), appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 7:07 AM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list when we pulled it. The Newsom card got the trend bonus. The Newsom, 'fine people' and Michigan Wi-Fi queries had small baselines earlier in the week, so their acceleration indexes are maxed out; the Michigan query's 348.23× reflects a baseline of about 35 posts a day. The Medicare for All, Somali and Van Hollen queries already carried large daily volumes all week, which keeps their acceleration modest. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Evening-to-morning score changes also reflect the volume ceiling (16,901 this morning versus 26,979 last evening) and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The Newsom query requires Newsom plus a death-penalty term or 'Newscum,' so it catches news relays and Newsom's defenders. The tax query requires Democrats, Dems or Neal plus a tax-cut or tax-hike phrase, so it also catches state-level tax stories (Arizona's appeared in the sample) and Democratic posts. The Michigan Wi-Fi query requires a Wi-Fi term plus Dominion, tabulator, 'voting machine' or 'Martin Township,' so it also catches rebuttals. The Somali query catches news relays, rebuttals and posts about the Minnesota fraud cases. The audit query catches posts mocking the demand. The market query requires a market term plus 'Democrats' or 'blue wave,' so it also catches rebuttals and general market posts. The 'fine people' query also catches posts defending the original reading. The Rikers query also catches straight news posts and rebuttals. The Medicare for All query catches supporters, opponents and general health-care posts, and its 'M4A' term can catch unrelated uses. The Van Hollen query catches syndicated news posts. The Rubio query catches any post pairing 'democratic socialism' with Marxism or communism, including posts from other countries. Replies are included. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This morning we pulled fresh samples for the Newsom, tax, Michigan Wi-Fi, audit, 'fine people' and Medicare for All queries. The Somali, market, Rubio, Van Hollen and Rikers cards carry last evening's sentiment and say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

disinfo.caveatBody: New this morning: 'Newsom is letting killers go free' is false. The commutations would change 548 death sentences to life without the possibility of parole, and none has taken effect: the California Constitution requires the state Supreme Court to approve clemency for anyone with more than one felony conviction, and Newsom's office says it will wait for the court (The National News Desk). Trump's earlier figure of '563' death-row inmates does not match the 548 in the commutation; his new memorandum applies to federal cases and federal death sentences, not California's state death row (White House; AP). The Michigan Wi-Fi claim still has no official finding behind it: the voting system's federal certificate lists no wireless LAN or WAN (U.S. Election Assistance Commission), we found no reported result from the sheriff or CISA, and the bipartisan Board of State Canvassers certified Michigan's results on Nov. 23 (Michigan Department of State; Michigan Public). On the '95% on welfare' figure, KTTC found it 'needs context': Center for Immigration Studies data put Somali households in Minnesota receiving some form of welfare at 81%. 'Democrats are raising your taxes' is ahead of the facts: Rep. Richard Neal has announced hearings, not a bill, and any bill would face Trump's promised veto (POLITICO; X News). Carried over from last evening: the Michigan 'Chinese Wi-Fi radio next to a Dominion tabulator' claim does not show a tabulator was connected to anything. The Election Crime Bureau's own write-up says the tabulator model in use has no internal modem and the system is certified with no wireless technology, and the hotspot's name matches a consumer wireless-display adapter; Lead Stories rated Patrick Colbeck's earlier Election Day version Unsupported, and Michigan's Department of State called it 'complete nonsense.' The sheriff's review it cites has not reported findings. Trump's 'Somalians have completely taken over… Minnesota… almost 95% are on some form of welfare' is false on scale and unsupported on the number: Somali Minnesotans are roughly 1–2 percent of the state, and the state demographer's figure for any public assistance, mostly Medicaid, was 84% (FactCheck.org); PolitiFact found his earlier '92% don't work' wrong. 'Mamdani will pay families to house the criminals he releases' describes a real program in a misleading way: the Kinship Reentry Housing Program started in 2021, pays $500 a month for up to 12 months to families housing a relative coming home, and the plan would grow it from 50 to 300 families (New York Post; NYC Mayor's Office). 'Jessica Tarlov admitted the "very fine people" hoax' gets the narrow point right and the conclusion wrong. Trump did say he was 'not talking about the neo-Nazis and the white nationalists,' and Snopes rated the claim that he called them 'very fine people' False; but Snopes also notes the Unite the Right rally was conceived, led and attended by white supremacists, so 'very fine people on both sides' was itself inaccurate, and one commentator's podcast remark is not evidence that Democrats invented the quote. Bessent's 'the sell-off began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls' is his reading of the timing, not a measured cause; in the same answer he cited hawkish Fed remarks and tighter financial conditions (CBS News transcript), and coverage ties the drop to the AI sell-off, the Anthropic IPO and Nvidia's turmoil as well as to expected data-center rules (NPR; The Hill). Page Twenty One finds Trump's 'more than $6 trillion' roughly right on a total-market basis, 'Nasdaq down 20%' exaggerated (about 10.9% from the Nov. 3 close to Nov. 20) and '100% due to the Democrats' not supported. Trump's 'NASDAQ, by itself, is down 20%' since the Nov. 3 midterms is wrong. From the last close before the vote (Nov. 2) to Friday's close the Nasdaq Composite fell 10.1%, the S&P 500 8.4% and the Dow 7.4% (Mediaite; MODEL, checking Nasdaq index data); the Composite is 18.1% below its Oct. 6 record, and the Nasdaq-100 is 19.8% below its record. '100% due to the Democrats' leaves out the AI and chip sell-off and the turmoil at Nvidia that coverage ties last week's drop to (The Hill), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. The viral Marco Rubio 'Democratic socialism… is Marxism' video is from Feb. 24, 2020, when he was a senator commenting on Bernie Sanders's primary campaign (Political Wire; The Right Scoop), not a response to this month's election. 'El-Sayed abandoned Medicare for All' is overstated: he said on Meet the Press he supports Sanders's bill but prefers a version that keeps private plans available (NBC News; POLITICO). 'Forensic-audit all 50 states before certifying' is misleading. Every state already has a post-election audit procedure (NCSL, via Votebeat), Texas began its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the U.S. Senate race on Nov. 19 (Houston Public Media), and audits and certification are separate processes that can run in parallel (The Crosscheck, which rated the 'don't certify until verified' claim Misleading). Earlier viral fraud claims, a Houston 'FBI raid' and a Wyandot County, Ohio, tally error, were debunked by PolitiFact and AFP. 'Medicare for All saves 114,000 lives and $1 trillion a year' is a projection from a Yale preprint that has not been peer reviewed; about 51,300 of those lives come from reversing coverage cuts enacted since 2025, not from single-payer itself, and the model leaves out transition costs (Yale School of Public Health; Renaissance Physician). Trump's 'Democrats Hurt Stocks' chart gets the numbers right and the cause wrong. The S&P 500 did fall 8.7% from the Nov. 3 close to the Nov. 20 close, and total U.S.-listed market value fell about $7.7 trillion (Candid Dragon's chatter check), but stocks rallied the day after the results, Friday's drop is tied mainly to the Nvidia accounting-probe report and the AI sell-off (Reuters; CNBC), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. 'Democrats are importing immigrants to replace Black voters' is Stephen A. Smith's stated belief, not an established fact: the census does count every resident for House seats, as the Constitution requires, but noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections (18 U.S.C. § 611), and PolitiFact has rated the related claim that millions of immigrants are registering to vote Pants on Fire. 'Trump endorsed Medicare for All' is overstated: he reposted El-Sayed's 'TrumpCare' card and praised Democrats' health-care ideas but has not backed a bill. 'Mamdani is releasing thousands of criminals' and 'Mamdani is closing Rikers now' get the plan backward: it sets a target of no more than 4,100 people in custody by the end of 2032, reached through diversion and shorter case delays, keeps Rikers open until borough jails are built, and asks the City Council to move the legal deadline later, from August 2027 to 2032 (City of New York; City & State; Gothamist). 'The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives 1.6 million people green cards' is misleading.

The busiest hour was 5 PM Monday (1,054 posts). 'Newscum,' Trump's nickname for Newsom, was on the U.S. X trends list at about 7:07 AM ET Tuesday (2,790 posts), and a sample of 'Newscum' posts was almost entirely about the commutations. At a Justice Department event Monday with Attorney General Todd Blanche and victims' families, Trump attacked California Gov. Gavin Newsom's Nov. 5 decision to commute all 548 death sentences in the state to life without parole: 'He stood with the murderers and the child slayers' (AP; C-SPAN). He signed a memorandum directing the attorney general to seek federal jurisdiction and the death penalty in qualifying cases and to expedite federal executions (White House). The commutations have not taken effect: the California Constitution requires the state Supreme Court to approve clemency for anyone with more than one felony conviction, and Newsom's office says it will wait for the court (The National News Desk). The federal memo covers federal cases, not California's death row. Newsom replied in a video that Trump's Justice Department 'prosecutes his enemies and pardons his friends.'
talkingPoints: Newsom stood with the murderers and the child slayers, not the families.
He waited until two days after the election to overrule 548 jury verdicts.
California voters kept the death penalty twice, and Newsom ignored them.
Trump is making sure the worst killers still face justice.
Democrats care more about monsters than victims.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: President Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche (DOJ event), the White House ('mass clemency to depraved killers'), White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis, Rep. Vince Fong (R-Calif.), @EricLDaugh (28,060 views on one post), @PeggyDodson, @NathanielSami, and accounts reviving Trump's 'Newscum' nickname. Fresno and Kern County district attorneys gave the critique a law-enforcement voice.
narratives.whyItWorks: It pairs a real, sweeping decision (all 548 death sentences) with named victims, many of them children, and puts grieving families in the room. Crime and punishment is one of the few issues where the Right still out-polls Democrats, and a lame-duck governor many see as a 2028 candidate is an easy national target. The 'he hid it until after the election' line turns a policy disagreement into a story about honesty. It also lets the Right change the subject from the midterm losses to Democrats and crime.
narratives.audience: Crime-focused conservatives and victims' advocates; California Republicans and some prosecutors; swing voters who support the death penalty for the worst crimes; and 2028 opponents of Newsom on both sides.
narratives.counter: Don't defend the killers. Defend the facts and the families' right to finality. No one is being released: the sentences become life without parole, and the California Supreme Court must approve commutations for anyone with more than one felony, so none have taken effect. Trump's order covers federal cases, not California's death row. And point out the contrast Newsom drew himself: a president who pardons allies is lecturing others about mercy.

narratives.audience: Trump voters in red states Democrats flipped, especially Texas; 2020 'stop the steal' veterans; election-integrity activists who backed the SAVE America Act; and voters angry at Senate Republicans who want someone to act before January.
narratives.counter: Agree with the premise and then point to the receipts: every state already audits its results, and Texas, under a 2021 Republican-passed law, is running its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the very Senate race people are questioning. Ask what a 'forensic audit' would check that the canvass, the hand-count audit and the risk-limiting audit don't. Note that Trump called the result a 'protest vote' against Senate Republicans. Don't mock the people asking; show them the audit that's already happening and when it reports.

factChecks.detail: Center for Immigration Studies 2025 data show about 81% of Somali households in Minnesota receive some form of welfare (nearly 90% with children), with about 54% receiving food stamps and 73% with at least one member on Medicaid. High, and far above Minnesota-native households, but not 'almost 95%.' Trump provided no source.

factChecks.claim: 'Like 88%' of Somalis in Minnesota receive welfare (related Trump claim, Dec. 2025).
factChecks.detail: The White House gave FactCheck.org no evidence for the figure. Later data it added: 81% of Somali immigrant households (Center for Immigration Studies) and 84% of people reporting Somali ancestry (Minnesota state demographer) used some public assistance, mostly Medicaid. That is not the '95%' Trump posted on Nov. 22, 2026.

factChecks.claim: '92% [of Minnesota Somalis] don't work' (related Trump claim, Feb. 2026).
factChecks.detail: About 28% of Somalis in Minnesota aren't working, a smaller share than for Minnesotans overall; about 9 in 10 receive some public assistance, but those programs typically include low-wage workers.

narratives.amplifiers: Right: President Trump (a Truth Social chart titled 'Democrats Hurt Stocks,' posted 3:14 PM ET Saturday), @GuntherEagleman (119,550 views Friday), copy-paste accounts such as @SeanHannityStat and @NorthStarMIO, Bill Mitchell (per X News), Breitbart ('Markets Fear Democrat Communism'), and smaller reply accounts. X News summarized the 'blame game' and the corrections. News coverage of the sell-off: AP, Reuters, CNBC, NBC News and Axios.
narratives.whyItWorks: Markets are a scoreboard people check on their phones, and a red day right after an election invites a simple cause-and-effect story. Trump had predicted a crash if Democrats won, so the drop looks like a prophecy fulfilled to his base. There is a grain of truth to work with, because analysts do cite fear of Democratic limits on AI data centers, and retirement-account losses are personal and immediate. Few people will read past the headline to the Nvidia probe or the Anthropic IPO.
narratives.audience: Retirement savers and 401(k) holders, small investors who follow market influencers, Trump's base primed by his 'crash' prediction, and swing voters anxious about the economy.
narratives.counter: Democrats don't take power until January 3, 2027; Republicans still run Congress and the White House. Friday's drop was led by AI stocks: Nvidia fell 14% on an SEC accounting probe report and Anthropic fell after its record IPO (Reuters; CNBC). Fear of new data-center limits is one factor analysts name, so don't deny it; say it plainly, and point out the market also rallied the day after the election (The Crosscheck). Pivot to what voters asked for: lower costs, not a higher Nasdaq.

factChecks.claim: The Nasdaq is down 20% since the Democrats' Nov. 3 win
factChecks.detail: MODEL (Nov. 22), checking Nasdaq index closes: the Nasdaq Composite closed at 25,164.31 on Nov. 2, the last close before the vote, and at 22,617.73 on Nov. 20, a 10.1% drop. It is 18.1% below its Oct. 6 record close; the Nasdaq-100 is 19.8% below its record. Mediaite reported the same 10.1% figure. MODEL did not verify the $6 trillion figure.

factChecks.claim: Democrats hurt stocks: the S&P 500 dropped 8.7%, about $5.9 trillion, since Election Day.
factChecks.rating: Numbers check out; the cause is oversimplified (TDDR read of Candid Dragon's data)
factChecks.detail: Candid Dragon's chatter check found the S&P 500 fell 8.70% from the Nov. 3 close (7,568.92) to the Nov. 20 close (6,910.39), and total U.S.-listed market value fell about $7.67 trillion, so the dollar figure is, if anything, understated. But stocks rallied the day after the results (S&P 500 +1.58%), Democrats' wins were one factor in the Nov. 5 drop through fears of AI data-center limits, and Friday's Nov. 20 drop is tied mainly to an SEC accounting-probe report on Nvidia and the AI sell-off. The new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. FactCheck.org noted Trump also skipped the post-election rally when he blamed Democrats for an earlier drop.

factChecks.claim: Democrats caused the stock market crash.
factChecks.rating: Mixed (The Crosscheck, on the same claim about the Nov. 5 drop)
factChecks.detail: Reviewing the Nov. 5 sell-off, The Crosscheck rated the claim that the drop was 'based on the results of the Election' Mixed: reporting names Democrats' sweep as one driver through fears about AI data-center limits, but the market rallied 1.6% the day after the vote, the selling centered on AI stocks already sliding since October, and no newly elected Democrat had taken office. Friday's Nov. 20 drop was not separately rated; AP, Reuters and CNBC attribute it mainly to the Nvidia probe, the Anthropic IPO sell-off, rates and slowing AI earnings.

Then separate labels from policies: Medicare for All, a public option and lower drug prices are policies voters can judge on cost and care, and many countries with private markets and free elections have universal coverage. Point out that the incoming House picked a leader who opposes Medicare for All. Don't argue Marxist theory; talk about what the bill would cost a family.
